In 1930 roughly one in four people in the Czech lands spoke German. They lived almost entirely in a horseshoe around the edge — and the shape is not a coincidence.

Germans in Czechia, 1930 — a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ The dark rim traces mountains: the Ore Mountains in the northwest, the Bohemian Forest along the Bavarian border, the Sudetes in the northeast. Bohemia is a basin, and this is the wall around it.

2/ That's the explanation. From roughly the 12th century, Bohemian kings invited German-speaking settlers to clear and mine the uplands — the last land to be settled, because it was the hardest. The population map still shows the medieval invitation.
3/ Note the islands in the interior: Jihlava, and pockets near Brno and Olomouc. Those are mining and merchant towns, German-speaking enclaves in a Czech countryside, some of them founded on silver.

4/ These districts were also the industrial core — glass, textiles, porcelain, machinery. When the Depression hit export industries hardest after 1929, it hit here hardest, and radical politics arrived with the unemployment.

5/ The word for all of it, Sudetenland, is a modern coinage. The Sudetes are only the northeastern range. Stretching the name across the whole horseshoe made three scattered regions sound like one country waiting to be redeemed.

6/ In September 1938 Britain, France, Italy and Germany met at Munich and handed these districts to Germany. Czechoslovakia was not at the table. It lost its border fortifications, its mountains and most of its heavy industry in ten days.

7/ After 1945 the map was erased. Around three million German speakers were expelled under the framework agreed at Potsdam. A joint Czech-German historians' commission later put direct violent deaths in the range of 15,000 to 30,000; other estimates run higher.

8/ Today these are the least densely populated parts of Czechia, and the postwar decrees that governed the expulsions still surface in Czech and Austrian politics. Nobody who lived on this map is left. The map is.
